Poppy Playtime is a phenomenal series. It has the right amount of scary, there isn't too much, nor too little. what I really like about this game is that the puzzles are quite difficult without making them impossible to figure out. another thing is that when there is a glitch in the game, the developers fix it almost immediately. they stay right behind on fixing bugs to make their game run as best as it can. another thing that makes this game awesome is the graphics. The graphics get better every chapter. the first chapter and the second chapter has decent graphics. But chapters 3 and 4 have unbelievably great graphics, and I can only imagine what the graphics for the fifth chapter is gonna be like. this game also has the perfect amount of gameplay. The first game is pretty short, but the rest are perfect in the length of gameplay. however, the gameplay gets darker each chapter, which I enjoy, but parents out there may not want their younger kids to see that kind of stuff. So, parents if you're reading this you may want to watch the gameplay first before letting your younger children play this game. the first two games are not that dark, but things start getting dark in the third chapter. Highly recommended, and perfect for the games price.

It’s not easy to review a game that’s already taking the internet by storm without repeating what’s already been said!

Poppy Playtime is a new horror game of which only the first chapter (just under an hour) is available.

So, for the moment, it’s more of an introduction than a full game, and it’s also tricky to rate it on that basis, as many of the criteria are based on promises.

Well, an indie horror game with a memorable monster – we’ve seen that plenty of times before. So what makes PP such a promising prospect?

First off, what really stands out is the game’s overall execution. The ‘daylight horror’ setting, which reminds me of the student project Bewilder House from almost 10 years ago, is really well rendered. You get that unsettling feeling when faced with something that, in theory, seems quite cute (well, yes – forget haunted hospitals or other places we’ve visited a hundred times; let’s go and check out a toy factory, shall we?). 

Then there’s the opening premise: an anonymous letter followed by a cassette telling us that the factory’s employees have never left the premises since it closed 10 years ago. A clue? Follow the red flower… that’s certainly enough to intrigue us.

Oh yes, and those big hands… They’re your main weapon. Well, I say ‘weapon’, but the only thing you’ll actually have to do is solve puzzles (which promise to be tricky) whilst feeling a knot in your stomach as the game’s monster (or monsters…?) appears.

Because yes, the star here is Huggy, that scary, lanky giant (animated to perfection) who’ll be chasing you throughout this chapter. But something tells me he’s got a few friends to help him out down the line...

Poppy Playtime is a little horror game that I highly recommend for the glimpse it offers of what’s to come. Scares, puzzles, story – who knows what else the developers have in store for us. The team is quite small and the game is progressing at its own pace, but everything feels so well-crafted and shows such a love for the game that I dare to hope for even more!

Besides, the game is only €4, so go for it!)

I am telling everyone right now to stay as far away as possible from this game and to not support this absolute DICKHEAD of a developer team. But before I go on and rant, I will talk about the game more objectively first.

Imagine Portal, but without the portals, at least kind of. The entire gameplay (at least so far) is just going from puzzle to puzzle and occasionally something "scary" happens. 
I really like the idea of the little Grab Pack, you can theoretically make some really cool puzzles with this. Sadly, the puzzles so far are kind of brain dead and even people with a room temperature IQ would eventually be able to finish them. While Portal required you to actively use your brain, this game is just kind of, find the most optimal way from point A to point B. Something that everyone who uses their brain can solve in like half a minute, and everyone else with like 2 minutes of trial and error... (honestly, I saw people watch YouTube guides for... what people call "puzzles" in Resident Evil 8, so I don't know what I am expecting at this point)
Its basically just something for YouTubers to make videos about, to draw a younger audience to it. 
The game is not scary AT ALL, unless you're like 12... or a YouTuber, the puzzles are brain dead so kids don't get impatient and stop playing and the lore is intentionally mysterious and vague, so that kids can watch more videos of their favorite YouTubers trying to piece the lore together, giving the game even more popularity in the long run. 
Its similar to Bendy and the Ink Machine, if you think about it... except that at least Bendy and the Ink Machine actually had a good chapter 1... After BATIM gained its popularity and audience of children, it went from a really cool idea and a cool setting, to something... not all that great.
But like I said, at least that game had a cool chapter 1 to pull you in.
This game is just kind of mediocre right from the start. 
You are asked to pay 4€ for what is essentially something that should be a free demo. A demo that has basically nothing to offer, other than a proof of concept. A few dumbed down puzzles, some "hidden" lore in the form of colored tapes, a little chase sequence that is really bad and literally a single line of dialogue at the end from the character the game is named after. And to add to to this, you have to pay 5€ for each future chapter...
Overall this game is very mediocre and borderline bad, but fine, I guess, 5.5/10.
Now, 5.5/10 would mean that it would still be worthy of a recommendation. Well, to understand why I am telling everyone to stay as far away from this game as possible, I have to rant a little.

[h1]Poppy Playtime is a soulless cash grab.[/h1]
Never in my life have my first impressions of a game been so quickly confirmed before even playing a game. Long after the massive success of the FNAF series, many indie studios chased after that same crowd with cartoony horror monsters and games of their own. Bendy and the Ink Machine, Baldi's Basics, Hello Neighbor, and probably plenty more indie horrors that tried to catch the attention of kids for either fame or money. It's a very overflown market nowadays and when I originally saw Poppy Playtime, I thought it was just another attempt at getting MatPat's attention for a quick buck. However, after a recent controversy surrounding the dev team's decisions came to light, I just had to cover this game.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2719566635 
Before delving into the game's development, let's talk about what you're actually buying on Steam. Poppy Playtime is a 40 minute tech demo of a full game that you pay $5 for. I have always not been the biggest fan of episodic games considering they're prone to inconsistent quality in releases and potentially being an abandoned project. I especially don't like the avoidance of using the term "early access" when it perfectly describes what you're getting. Except you're paying even more for future updates. Reactions to completing Poppy Playtime has always been a mere "That's it? You're serious?" from let's players and friends alike. And that 40 minute tech demo is not even good to begin with. It has a puzzle count that doesn't even break into the double digits and a singular chase scene. The game's unique gimmick is that you have these long arms that you use to connect one thing to another thing. Really innovating and impressive that this video game has long arms. The only thing these stretchy arms achieved in doing was annoying me that it was inconsistent on if the game let me pick things up with my bare hands or my gimmicky stretchy hands. A fucking basic action in a video game becoming tedious isn't a genius idea or masterpiece in game design. The soundtrack is nearly non-existent and what is there is incredibly generic for the horror genre. The graphics are alright but the environmental areas are so empty and structured with no care in mind that they feel so much like a video game level, really killing the immersion which is obviously very important for a horror game. Everything in this game is all so generic and cliche, I honestly have no idea how to explain the praise behind this game other than that they're the same kids who just got into FNAF. Which isn't the issue of this game, keep in mind.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2719564398
Poppy Playtime also fails as a horror game. Horror is probably the genre with the largest amount of bad movies and games considering it's an extremely difficult feeling to pull off. Video games have an advantage over movies when it comes to this since there's player interaction and the consequences fall onto the player rather than on a character in the plot. Poppy Playtime doesn't really have either of those since as mentioned earlier, there's a single chase scene. The entirety of the game has no dark or spooky atmosphere or tense moments. Also the monster isn't even close to being scary! I'm sorry but every time I think my scrawny self could take a stuffed animal in a fight, I lose a lot of the spook factor. There's also a large amount of invincibility you have when you encounter the blue creep, so you can just walk right into him for a bit. Oh and the chase scene feels incredibly scripted, almost forgot that. Even the jumpscare isn't scary! How do you screw that up? Jumpscares are the easiest thing to pull off in horror, so much so that it's a common cheap trick pulled by directors. The only people who will get scared by this game are babies. And again, horror for kids isn't the issue. It's one thing to buy a bad game. It's whole other issue if it's a bad game trying to milk kids for money.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2719564107
Now let's get into what actually brought this game to my attention: NFTs, or Non Fungible Tokens. They're probably something people following the gaming industry are unfortunately becoming more and more aware of. The way they're implemented in video games currently serves the same purpose as cosmetic microtransactions except they're way more expensive and they come with a url that says you own the item. Someone had to compare the entire world playing video games, watching tv, and using the internet combined to make the energy usage of a single NFT blockchain look "good". Poppy Playtime offers their own NFTs for a grand total of $90 for digital "trading cards" and they are said to be required for a puzzle solution in the next chapter. That coupled with the fact that both chapters will cost $5 makes Poppy Playtime a game worth a grand total of at least $100. It's even worse that this stuff is targeted specifically towards children and they aren't exactly known to make the smartest financial decisions. And yes, despite being a horror game, Poppy Playtime is marketed for a child audience. There's no blood or gore or anything overtly mature that would lead to an M-rating if a physical release ever happened. That and the YouTube channel of the creators is filled with videos combining franchises like Among Us, FNAF, Friday Night Funkin, and other internet sensations with massive kid followings. It was honestly a trip having my every preconceived notion about the developers the moment the game blew up confirmed through the minimal amount of research.

[b]I honestly don't think I can give this game a score higher than a 0/10.[/b] It's not scary, it's got really boring puzzles, it's not even a complete experience, and its only claim to fame is checking all the boxes for MatPat to make a video on it. Oh and no one should ever pay $90 for digital trading cards that you don't even own just to solve a puzzle. The only fear I've got from playing this game was the amount of money children have wasted on the NFTs and how many more will when they inevitably pull the same trick with the next few chapters. Also as final note, don't bully the kids who end up liking the game.
